e-564.knowledge_point: Finding the Time Intervals on which a Particle is Moving in a Particular Direction
e-564.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 3t^2+2t-6,$ where $t > 0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle is stationary when $t=0\,\textrm s,$ determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving to the right.
e-564.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+2t-6)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+{t}^{2}-6t+C\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the particle is stationary at the time $t=0.$ This means $v(0) = 0,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(0)^{3}+(0)^{2}-6(0)+C \\ 0 & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore the velocity of the particle is

$$
v(t) = t^3+t^2-6t.
$$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v > 0.$ This gives

$$
t^3+t^2-6t = t(t+3)(t-2) > 0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094076/assets/03b5ff6282d59038cbb355c0c3f017b544f286228ba4c3a82329897b4b43674c.png)

The particle moves to the right when $v(t)$ is positive. So, from the graph, we see that the particle moves to the right when $t>2.$

e-565.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
e-565.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 6t-3t^2,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=1\,\textrm s,$ calculate the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
e-565.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d t} = a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t) = 0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t) = 0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6t-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3t(2-t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t> 0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t = 2\,\textrm s.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =6-6t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =6-6(2) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Since $v''(2) <      0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\textrm s.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3(1)^{2}-(1)^{3}+C & =2 \\ 3-1+C & =2\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) =3t^2-t^3.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
v_{\text{max}}= v(2) = 3(2)^2 - (2)^3 =4\,\textrm m / \textrm s
$$

So the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ is reached at $t=2\,\textrm s.$

e-7226.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle is Stationary
e-7226.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) =2t-6$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=1\,\textrm s$, determine the moments in time when the particle is stationary.
e-7226.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\textrm m / \textrm s.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-6)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-6t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) =4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =(1)^{2}-6(1)+C \\ 4 & =-5+C \\ C & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = t^2-6t + 9.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\textrm m / \textrm s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-6t+9 & =0 \\ (t-3)^{2} & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=3 \,\textrm s.$

after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=1-2t$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity $v=-6\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=4\,\text{s}$, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the right.
after.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(4)=-6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =(4)-(4)^{2}+C \\ -6 & =4-16+C \\ -6 & =-12+C \\ C & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-{t}^{2}+t+6.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v>0.$ This gives

$$
-{t}^{2}+t+6=-({t}^{2}-t-6)=-(t+2)(t-3)>0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

after.html:
Question 5
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=1−2t, where t>0 is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity v=−6m/s when t=4s, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the right.

a
 t>6
b
 3<t<6
c
 2<t<4
d
 t>3
e
 0<t<3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(1−2t)dt=t−t2+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(4)=−6. Substituting this into the above gives −6=(4)−(4)2+C−6=4−16+C−6=−12+CC=6.

Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=−t2+t+6.

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the right, we must solve the inequality v>0. This gives

−t2+t+6=−(t2−t−6)=−(t+2)(t−3)>0.

Plotting the graph of v(t), we get the following picture.

From the graph, we see that v>0 whenever 0<t<3.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Time Intervals on which a Particle is Moving in a Particular Direction
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=1-2t$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity $v=-6\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=4\,\text{s}$, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the right.
content.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(4)=-6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =(4)-(4)^{2}+C \\ -6 & =4-16+C \\ -6 & =-12+C \\ C & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-{t}^{2}+t+6.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v>0.$ This gives

$$
-{t}^{2}+t+6=-({t}^{2}-t-6)=-(t+2)(t-3)>0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094076/assets/74db16dc00f5d08637cef02960409b7fd15c4bd3c19f577fa5a1f30ac8c402d3.png)

From the graph, we see that $v>0$ whenever $0<t<3.$

Question 6
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=12−3t2, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=15m/s when t=1s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=16m/s,t=2s
b
vmax=28m/s,t=2s
c
vmax=13m/s,t=3s
d
vmax=15m/s,t=1s
e
vmax=20m/s,t=2s
Submit

decision.explanation: Since v'(t)=12-3t^2 is positive for 0<t<2 and negative for t>2, velocity reaches its maximum at t=2. Integrating gives v(t)=12t-t^3+C; v(1)=15 implies C=4. Thus v(2)=24-8+4=20 m/s.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=12-3{t}^{2},$ where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=15\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 12-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3(2-t)(2+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =-6t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =-6(2) \\  & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(2)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (12-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =12t-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=15.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}12(1)-(1)^{3}+C & =15 \\ 11+C & =15\,⟹\,C=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4+12t-{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(2)=4+12(2)-(2)^{3}=20\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

\begin{aligned}12(1)-(1)^{3}+C & =15 \\ 11+C & =15\,⟹\,C=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4+12t-{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(2)=4+12(2)-(2)^{3}=20\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

Question 7
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=6cos⁡(2t), where t≥0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=1m/s when t=0s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the earliest time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=4m/s,t=π4s
b
 vmax=1m/s,t=π3s
c
 vmax=3m/s,t=π4s
d
 vmax=3m/s,t=π2s
e
 vmax=4m/s,t=π2s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating acceleration and using v(0)=1 gives v(t)=3 sin(2t)+1. Its maximum is 4 m/s, attained when sin(2t)=1. The earliest nonnegative time is 2t=π/2, so t=π/4 s.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the earliest time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. 

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for $t>0,$ are

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{4},…
$$

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-12\cdot 1 \\  & =-12<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\text{d}t \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+C & =1 \\ 0+C & =1\,⟹\,C=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(\frac{\pi }{4})=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}.
$$

So the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached first time at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

after.html:
Question 7
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=6cos⁡(2t), where t≥0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=1m/s when t=0s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the earliest time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=4m/s,t=π4s
b
 vmax=1m/s,t=π3s
c
 vmax=3m/s,t=π4s
d
 vmax=3m/s,t=π2s
e
 vmax=4m/s,t=π2s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The extrema of the velocity v occur at the critical points of v.

Since dvdt=a(t), to find the times where v is a maximum, we just need to solve a(t)=0 and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving a(t)=0 gives

a(t)=06cos⁡(2t)=0cos⁡(2t)=02t=π2+πnt=π4+π2n,

where n is any integer.

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for t>0, are t=π4,3π4,5π4,…

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of v(t):

d2vdt2=ddt(dvdt)=ddt(a(t))=ddt(6cos⁡2t)=−12sin⁡2t.

At t=π4, the second derivative is

v″(π4)=−12sin⁡(2⋅π4)=−12sin⁡(π2)=−12⋅1=−12<0.

Since v″(π4)<0, we conclude that the velocity is maximized when t=π4. Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is t=π4s.

Now, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫6cos⁡(2t)dt=3sin⁡(2t)+C. To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=1. Substituting this into the above gives 3sin⁡(0)+C=10+C=1⟹C=1. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=1+3sin⁡(2t).

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

vmax=v(π4)=1+3sin⁡(2⋅π4)=4m/s.

So the maximum velocity vmax=4m/s is reached first time at t=π4s.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the earliest time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
content.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. 

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for $t>0,$ are

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{4},…
$$

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-12\cdot 1 \\  & =-12<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\text{d}t \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+C & =1 \\ 0+C & =1\,⟹\,C=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(\frac{\pi }{4})=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}.
$$

So the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached first time at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+C & =1 \\ 0+C & =1\,⟹\,C=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(\frac{\pi }{4})=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}.
$$

So the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached first time at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

The extrema of the velocity v occur at the critical points of v.

Since dvdt=a(t), to find the times where v is a maximum, we just need to solve a(t)=0 and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving a(t)=0 gives

a(t)=06cos⁡(2t)=0cos⁡(2t)=02t=π2+πnt=π4+π2n,

where n is any integer.

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for t>0, are t=π4,3π4,5π4,…

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of v(t):

d2vdt2=ddt(dvdt)=ddt(a(t))=ddt(6cos⁡2t)=−12sin⁡2t.

At t=π4, the second derivative is

v″(π4)=−12sin⁡(2⋅π4)=−12sin⁡(π2)=−12⋅1=−12<0.

Since v″(π4)<0, we conclude that the velocity is maximized when t=π4. Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is t=π4s.

Now, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫6cos⁡(2t)dt=3sin⁡(2t)+C. To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=1. Substituting this into the above gives 3sin⁡(0)+C=10+C=1⟹C=1. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=1+3sin⁡(2t).

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

vmax=v(π4)=1+3sin⁡(2⋅π4)=4m/s.

So the maximum velocity vmax=4m/s is reached first time at t=π4s.

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=4−t2, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=0m/s when t=0s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=163m/s,t=2s
b
vmax=83m/s,t=2s
c
vmax=113m/s,t=1s
d
vmax=13m/s,t=1s
e
vmax=143m/s,t=2s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating and using v(0)=0 gives v(t)=4t-t^3/3. Since v'(t)=4-t^2 is positive for 0<t<2 and negative for t>2, the maximum occurs at t=2 s. Its value is v(2)=8-8/3=16/3 m/s.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=4-{t}^{2}$, where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 4-{t}^{2} & =0 \\ (2-t)(2+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t⩾0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2}) \\  & =-2t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =-2(2) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(2)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (4-{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0)-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{3}+C & =0 \\ 0+0+C & =0\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(2)=4(2)-\frac{1}{3}(2)^{3}=\frac{16}{3}\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

Question 8
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=4−t2, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=0m/s when t=0s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=163m/s,t=2s
b
vmax=83m/s,t=2s
c
vmax=113m/s,t=1s
d
vmax=13m/s,t=1s
e
vmax=143m/s,t=2s
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The extrema of the velocity v occur at the critical points of v.

Since dvdt=a(t), to find the times where v is a maximum, we just need to solve a(t)=0 and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving a(t)=0 gives

a(t)=04−t2=0(2−t)(2+t)=0t=±2.

Since t⩾0, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when t=2s.

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of v(t) and evaluate it at t=2:

v″(t)=d2vdt2=ddt(dvdt)=ddt(a(t))=ddt(4−t2)=−2tv″(2)=−2(2)=−4.

Since v″(2)<0, we conclude that the velocity is maximized when t=2s.

Now, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(4−t2)dt=4t−13t3+C To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=0. Substituting this into the above gives 4(0)−13(0)3+C=00+0+C=0⟹C=0. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=4t−13t3.

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

vmax=v(2)=4(2)−13(2)3=163m/s

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=4-{t}^{2}$, where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
content.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 4-{t}^{2} & =0 \\ (2-t)(2+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t⩾0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2}) \\  & =-2t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =-2(2) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(2)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (4-{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0)-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{3}+C & =0 \\ 0+0+C & =0\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(2)=4(2)-\frac{1}{3}(2)^{3}=\frac{16}{3}\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

vmax=v(2)=4(2)−13(2)3=163m/s

Your Answer:
vmax=83m/s,t=2s

If the particle has velocity v=4m/s when t=0s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=293m/s,t=1s
b
vmax=7m/s,t=3s
c
vmax=13m/s,t=2s
d
vmax=4m/s,t=3s
e
vmax=203m/s,t=2s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating and using v(0)=4 gives v(t)=4+2t-t^2/3. Acceleration is zero at t=3 and changes from positive to negative there, so velocity is maximized at t=3 s. Then v(3)=4+6-3=7 m/s.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=2-\frac{2}{3}t,$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 2-\frac{2}{3}t & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-\frac{2}{3}t) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(3)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2-\frac{2}{3}t)\text{d}t \\  & =2t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{2}+C & =4 \\ 0+0+C & =4\,⟹\,C=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{2}+4.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(3)=2(3)-\frac{1}{3}(3)^{2}+4=7\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

after.html:
Question 9
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=2−23t, where t⩾0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=4m/s when t=0s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=293m/s,t=1s
b
vmax=7m/s,t=3s
c
vmax=13m/s,t=2s
d
vmax=4m/s,t=3s
e
vmax=203m/s,t=2s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The extrema of the velocity v occur at the critical points of v.

Since dvdt=a(t), to find the times where v is a maximum, we just need to solve a(t)=0 and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving a(t)=0 gives

a(t)=02−23t=0t=3.

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when t=3s.

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of v(t) d2vdt2=ddt(dvdt)=ddt(a(t))=ddt(2−23t)=−23.

Since v″(3)<0, we conclude that the velocity is maximized when t=3s.

Now, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(2−23t)dt=2t−13t2+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=4. Substituting this into the above gives 2(0)−13(0)2+C=40+0+C=4⟹C=4. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=2t−13t2+4.

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

vmax=v(3)=2(3)−13(3)2+4=7m/s

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=2-\frac{2}{3}t,$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
content.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 2-\frac{2}{3}t & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-\frac{2}{3}t) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(3)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2-\frac{2}{3}t)\text{d}t \\  & =2t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{2}+C & =4 \\ 0+0+C & =4\,⟹\,C=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{2}+4.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(3)=2(3)-\frac{1}{3}(3)^{2}+4=7\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

before.html:
Question 10
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=6−2t, where t⩾0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=2m/s when t=1s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=9m/s,t=3s
b
vmax=6m/s,t=3s
c
vmax=6m/s,t=2s
d
vmax=12m/s,t=3s
e
vmax=9m/s,t=2s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=6t-t^2+C. Using v(1)=2 gives C=-3, so v(t)=6-(t-3)^2. Thus the maximum velocity is 6 m/s at t=3 s.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6-2t,$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6-2t & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6-2t) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(3)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6-2t)\text{d}t \\  & =6t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6(1)-(1)^{2}+C & =2 \\ 6-1+C & =2\,⟹\,C=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-{t}^{2}+6t-3.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(3)=-(3)^{2}+6(3)-3=6\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

Question 10
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=6−2t, where t⩾0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=2m/s when t=1s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=9m/s,t=3s
b
vmax=6m/s,t=3s
c
vmax=6m/s,t=2s
d
vmax=12m/s,t=3s
e
vmax=9m/s,t=2s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The extrema of the velocity v occur at the critical points of v.

Since dvdt=a(t), to find the times where v is a maximum, we just need to solve a(t)=0 and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving a(t)=0 gives

a(t)=06−2t=0t=3.

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when t=3s.

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of v(t) d2vdt2=ddt(dvdt)=ddt(a(t))=ddt(6−2t)=−2.

Since v″(3)<0, we conclude that the velocity is maximized when t=3s.

Now, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(6−2t)dt=6t−t2+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(1)=2. Substituting this into the above gives 6(1)−(1)2+C=26−1+C=2⟹C=−3. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=−t2+6t−3.

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

vmax=v(3)=−(3)2+6(3)−3=6m/s

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6-2t,$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
content.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6-2t & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6-2t) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(3)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6-2t)\text{d}t \\  & =6t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6(1)-(1)^{2}+C & =2 \\ 6-1+C & =2\,⟹\,C=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-{t}^{2}+6t-3.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(3)=-(3)^{2}+6(3)-3=6\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

Question 11
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=t1/3−1, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=4m/s when t=8s, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.

a
t=6427s
b
t=163s
c
t=139s
d
t=934s
e
t=332s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=(3/4)t^{4/3}-t+C. Since v(8)=4, we get 4=12-8+C, so C=0. For t>0, v(t)=t((3/4)t^{1/3}-1)=0 requires t^{1/3}=4/3. Thus t=64/27 s.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)={t}^{1/3}-1,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=8\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ({t}^{1/3}-1)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(8)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =\frac{3}{4}(8)^{4/3}-8+C \\ 4 & =12-8+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t & =0 \\ t(\frac{3}{4}{t}^{1/3}-1) & =0 \\ t & =0,\frac{64}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=t1/3−1, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=4m/s when t=8s, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.

a
t=6427s
b
t=163s
c
t=139s
d
t=934s
e
t=332s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particle is stationary when v=0m/s.

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(t1/3−1)dt=34t4/3−t+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(8)=4. Substituting this into the above gives 4=34(8)4/3−8+C4=12−8+CC=0. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=34t4/3−t.

Now, we find the moments in time when v=0m/s:

34t4/3−t=0t(34t1/3−1)=0t=0,6427.

Since t>0, we discard the solution t=0. Therefore, the particle is stationary when t=6427s.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle is Stationary
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)={t}^{1/3}-1,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=8\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
content.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ({t}^{1/3}-1)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(8)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =\frac{3}{4}(8)^{4/3}-8+C \\ 4 & =12-8+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4/3}-t & =0 \\ t(\frac{3}{4}{t}^{1/3}-1) & =0 \\ t & =0,\frac{64}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ we discard the solution $t=0.$ Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{64}{27}\,\text{s}.$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=-\frac{4}{{t}^{2}},$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=\frac{1}{3}\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=4\,\text{s},$  determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int -\frac{4}{{t}^{2}}\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(4)=\frac{1}{3}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & =\frac{4}{(4)}+C \\ \frac{1}{3} & =1+C \\ C & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{4}{t}-\frac{2}{3}.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{t}-\frac{2}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{4}{t} & =\frac{2}{3} \\ t & =\frac{12}{2} \\ t & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=6\,\text{s}.$

Question 12
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=−4t2, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=13m/s when t=4s, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.

a
t=4s
b
t=2s
c
t=0s
d
t=3s
e
t=6s
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The particle is stationary when v=0m/s.

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫−4t2dt=4t+C To determine C, we use the fact that v(4)=13. Substituting this into the above gives 13=4(4)+C13=1+CC=−23. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=4t−23.

Now, we find the moments in time when v=0m/s:

4t−23=04t=23t=122t=6

Therefore, the particle is stationary when t=6s.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution declares t=6 s, matching option e. This agrees with v(t)=4/t-2/3, which equals zero at t=6. The deliberately incorrect submission selected t=3 s.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle is Stationary
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=-\frac{4}{{t}^{2}},$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=\frac{1}{3}\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=4\,\text{s},$  determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
content.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int -\frac{4}{{t}^{2}}\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(4)=\frac{1}{3}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & =\frac{4}{(4)}+C \\ \frac{1}{3} & =1+C \\ C & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{4}{t}-\frac{2}{3}.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{t}-\frac{2}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{4}{t} & =\frac{2}{3} \\ t & =\frac{12}{2} \\ t & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=6\,\text{s}.$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=9\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(9)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\sqrt{9}+C \\ 1 & =3+C \\ C & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\sqrt{t}-2.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{t}-2 & =0 \\ \sqrt{t} & =2 \\ t & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\sqrt{t}-{t}^{3/2}$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=\frac{4}{15}\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\sqrt{t}-{t}^{3/2})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{4}{15}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{15} & =\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}(1)^{5/2}+C \\ \frac{4}{15} & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{5}+C \\ \frac{4}{15} & =\frac{4}{15}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5/2}=0 \\ \frac{2}{5}{t}^{3/2}(\frac{5}{3}-t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0$, the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{5}{3}\,\text{s}.$

$$
